nodes.title: 패러다임의 전환: 범용 클라우드에서 AI 전용 인프라로
nodes.summary:
This section introduces the paradigm shift from general-purpose cloud infrastructure to AI-native infrastructure. It explains that traditional data center architecture — built on CPU-centric sequential processing, air cooling, Ethernet networking, and transaction-oriented storage — has hit physical and structural limits as generative AI and LLM parameter counts have grown exponentially, making simple scale-out approaches inefficient in both compute and cost.

A comparison table (Table 1-1) contrasts general-purpose and AI-dedicated data centers across seven dimensions: compute architecture (CPU sequential vs. GPU/NPU massively parallel), rack power density (5–15kW vs. 40–120kW+), cooling (air vs. direct liquid/immersion), intra-node interconnect (PCIe at tens of GB/s vs. NVLink at 900GB/s+), inter-node network fabric (Ethernet 10–100Gbps vs. InfiniBand/RoCE 400Gbps+), storage patterns (small random transactions vs. large sequential streaming I/O), and total power scale (single-digit-to-tens of MW vs. hundreds of MW with dedicated power infrastructure).

It then examines the structural causes of performance degradation in large-scale clusters, focusing on communication and synchronization overhead. Because AI training requires global All-Reduce synchronization of gradients across nodes, computation halts during data exchange; as node counts rise, communication paths and exchange complexity grow exponentially. Standard Ethernet-based hierarchical network architectures fail to contain the resulting latency, sharply degrading inter-accelerator synchronization efficiency and producing a "performance saturation" state where adding compute resources no longer yields proportional gains in training speed.

nodes.summary:
This section (Chapter 1.2) explains the paradigm shift from general-purpose cloud infrastructure to AI-native infrastructure.

**Main points:**

1. **Why the shift is happening** — Conventional data centers were built on CPU-centric sequential compute, air cooling, Ethernet networking, and transaction-oriented storage. The explosive growth of generative AI/LLMs has exposed the physical and structural limits of that design; scale-out by simply adding servers has hit a ceiling in both compute efficiency and cost.

2. **Comparison table (Table 1-1)** contrasting general-purpose vs. AI-dedicated data centers across seven dimensions: compute architecture (CPU sequential vs. GPU/NPU massively parallel), rack power density (5–15kW vs. 40–120kW+), cooling (air vs. direct liquid/immersion), intra-node interconnect (PCIe tens of GB/s vs. NVLink 900GB/s+), inter-node fabric (Ethernet 10–100Gbps vs. InfiniBand/RoCE 400Gbps+), storage pattern (small random transactions vs. large sequential streaming I/O), and power scale (MW-scale vs. hundreds of MW with dedicated power infrastructure).

3. **Section 1.2.1 — Four structural causes of large-cluster performance degradation:**
   - *Communication/synchronization overhead* — All-Reduce gradient synchronization stalls compute; hierarchical Ethernet fabrics can't contain latency growth as node count rises, producing a performance-saturation point where added compute doesn't yield proportional speedup.
   - *Data starvation* — Storage read throughput fails to keep pace with accelerator speed, leaving expensive compute idle.
   - *Checkpointing write bottleneck* — Multi-TB checkpoints from trillion-parameter models written simultaneously by thousands of nodes exceed storage controller bandwidth, consuming roughly 10–25% of total training time in write waits.
   - *Cooling limits from power density* — Air cooling can't handle AI rack heat density; thermal throttling worsens tail latency, dragging the whole cluster down to the slowest node.

4. **Section 1.2.2 — AI-dedicated infrastructure requirements** (five technical layers, of which two are covered in this excerpt): physical infrastructure design for high-density power and thermal management (floor load-bearing for heavy racks, large-scale power delivery, high-availability power for non-stop operation, space efficiency and serviceability), and ultra-high-density power supply paired with next-generation liquid cooling (needed for 60kW+ per rack, removing chip-level heat immediately to guarantee throttle-free sustained performance).

nodes.title: Compute Fabric 아키텍처
nodes.summary:
This section covers NHN FactoryX's GPU cluster system architecture, focusing on three areas:

**Cluster hierarchy (2.1.1)** — The cluster is built from standardized GPU nodes (building blocks) repeated in a scalable-unit design for predictable performance and consistent automation. It defines four layers — Node (single GPU server, NVLink-joined), Scalable Unit (several to dozens of nodes forming a non-blocking domain under one InfiniBand switch layer), Pod/Block (multiple scalable units linked via spine switches, the unit of operation, isolation, and multi-tenancy), and Cluster (a set of Pods sharing a common control plane and storage plane). Higher layers mean more switch hops and stronger isolation, so distributed training jobs should be placed to complete communication within the lowest possible layer; NCCL and other collective libraries exploit this topology information.

**Compute Fabric architecture (2.1.2)** — Three physically separated fabrics: Compute Fabric (East-West GPU↔GPU, handling All-Reduce/All-Gather over InfiniBand or RoCEv2 rail-optimized topology), Storage Fabric (dataset and checkpoint I/O with GPUDirect Storage and parallel file systems bypassing the CPU), and Management/In-band Fabric (orchestration, monitoring, logging on ordinary Ethernet). Physical separation prevents traffic interference, allows per-fabric tuning (lossless/low-latency vs. throughput/queue management vs. compatibility/visibility), and isolates fault impact.

**Topology (2.1.3)** — Because AI clusters are dominated by simultaneous collective communication, the interconnect uses Fat-Tree non-blocking or 1:1 subscribed designs, with uniform uplinks from every leaf to spine guaranteeing equal effective bandwidth and path diversity. Rail-Optimized wiring aligns the Nth GPU in each node to the same Nth leaf switch group, so same-index GPU traffic (e.g., tensor-parallel All-Reduce) completes within a single switch layer — reducing hop latency and congestion, and easing the communication bottleneck that degrades GPU utilization.

nodes.title: 토폴로지: Fat-Tree 기반 Rail-Optimized 설계
nodes.summary:
This section covers AI cluster network architecture, specifically fabric separation and interconnect topology design.

**Fabric separation (three planes):**
- **Compute Fabric (East-West, GPU↔GPU)** — handles collective communication (All-Reduce, All-Gather) during distributed training, built on InfiniBand or RoCEv2 with a Rail-Optimized topology
- **Storage Fabric** — handles training dataset and checkpoint I/O, connected to GPUDirect Storage (GDS)-capable parallel file systems for a CPU-bypass path
- **Management/In-band Fabric** — a general Ethernet plane for orchestration, monitoring, and log collection, physically isolated from compute traffic

**Rationale for physical separation:** large-scale collective communication is shielded from interference by storage I/O and management traffic; each fabric can be tuned independently for its own traffic pattern (lossless/ultra-low latency for compute, high throughput and stable queue management for storage, broad compatibility and operational visibility for management); and failure domains are isolated per fabric so one plane's problem doesn't degrade whole-cluster availability.

**Topology (2.1.3): Fat-Tree based Rail-Optimized design**
- AI cluster interconnects differ from ordinary data centers because collective communication — all GPUs transmitting simultaneously — dominates, so the design principle is a non-blocking or 1:1 subscribed Fat-Tree
- **Fat-Tree** widens link bandwidth toward upper tiers to guarantee equal effective bandwidth between any two nodes; uniform leaf-to-spine uplink counts preserve path-selection freedom regardless of traffic pattern and structurally mitigate link hotspots
- **Rail-Optimized** aligns NIC cabling so the Nth GPU in each node always connects to the same Nth leaf switch group, letting same-index GPU traffic (e.g., Tensor Parallel All-Reduce) complete within a single switch tier — reducing spine hop latency and congestion, shortening collective communication end-to-end latency, and easing the communication bottleneck that drives down GPU utilization

nodes.title: 고속 인터커넥트
nodes.summary:
This section covers high-speed interconnects in AI system architecture, arguing that interconnect performance is part of compute performance rather than mere networking — and that imbalance between intra-node and inter-node bandwidth sharply degrades overall GPU utilization.

**Intra-node (NVLink / NVSwitch):** NVLink is NVIDIA's dedicated GPU-to-GPU link offering an order of magnitude more bandwidth and lower latency than PCIe; NVSwitch aggregates those links so any GPU pair gets equal bandwidth. NHN FactoryX's standard GPU node uses an NVSwitch-based full-mesh topology, so any two GPUs communicate through a single NVSwitch hop — eliminating distance-dependent performance variance in communication-heavy strategies like Tensor Parallel. With NVLink 5/NVSwitch 4, this extends beyond a single node to the NVL72 rack domain, making 72 GPUs act as one communication domain. A generation table lists per-GPU aggregate bandwidth: NVLink 3/NVSwitch 2 at 600 GB/s bidirectional (A100), NVLink 4/NVSwitch 3 at 900 GB/s (H100/H200), and NVLink 5/NVSwitch 4 at 1,800 GB/s (B200/GB200).

**Inter-node (InfiniBand):** InfiniBand is the standard for node-to-node traffic, chosen for three properties rather than raw bandwidth — RDMA for CPU-bypass, microsecond-latency access to remote memory (directly affecting throughput and GPU utilization since distributed-training communication is GPU-memory-to-GPU-memory movement); Adaptive Routing, where switches dynamically reroute based on real-time congestion to spread All-Reduce hotspots, outperforming static routing in synchronized collective patterns; and SHARP in-network computing, which executes part of collective operations inside the switch to cut network round trips and end-to-end latency.

This section covers high-speed interconnect design for AI/GPU clusters, treating interconnect bandwidth as part of compute performance rather than mere networking. It's organized into three parts:

**Intra-node (NVLink/NVSwitch):** NVLink provides direct GPU-to-GPU links with an order of magnitude more bandwidth and lower latency than PCIe, while NVSwitch aggregates those links so any GPU pair gets equal bandwidth. NHN FactoryX's standard GPU node adopts an NVSwitch-based Full-Mesh topology where any two GPUs communicate through a single NVSwitch hop, eliminating distance-based performance variance for communication-heavy strategies like Tensor Parallel. A generation table lists NVLink 3/NVSwitch 2 (600GB/s bidirectional, A100), NVLink 4/NVSwitch 3 (900GB/s, H100/H200), and NVLink 5/NVSwitch 4 (1,800GB/s, B200/GB200), with the newest generation extending the single-node communication domain across a full NVL72 rack of 72 GPUs.

**Inter-node (InfiniBand):** InfiniBand is the standard for node-to-node traffic, chosen for three properties beyond raw bandwidth — RDMA (bypassing the CPU for microsecond-level latency and higher GPU utilization), Adaptive Routing (dynamic congestion-aware path reassignment to spread All-Reduce hotspots), and SHARP in-network computing (performing part of collective operations inside the switch to cut round trips and end-to-end latency). A table maps generations to bandwidth and recommended NIC counts: HDR (200Gbps, A100, 4–8 NICs/node), NDR (400Gbps, H100/H200, 8 NICs/node with one per rail), and XDR (800Gbps, B200/GB200).

**Balance principles:** From a full-stack view, interconnect must be designed as a set of balance ratios rather than single bandwidth figures, since a shortfall in any segment raises the communication share of distributed training and sharply degrades GPU utilization. The three key variables are the intra-node vs. inter-node bandwidth ratio (Tensor Parallel leans on NVLink; Pipeline/Data Parallel lean on InfiniBand, so the target ratio depends on the dominant parallelism strategy), per-GPU NIC bandwidth (below a certain ratio to GPU memory bandwidth, All-Reduce becomes communication-bound), and oversubscription ratio (1:1 non-blocking Leaf-Spine as the principle, never exceeding 1:2, since higher oversubscription accumulates spine congestion and produces measurable interference between training jobs).

nodes.title: 전력 및 냉각 설계
nodes.summary:
This section (2.3 of a systems-architecture document) covers power and cooling design for AI data centers, focusing on why air cooling breaks down as rack density climbs past 60kW. It opens by outlining the section's scope: the structural limits of air cooling, Direct-to-Chip (D2C) liquid cooling as the replacement mechanism and its validation requirements, design parameters at the CDU/manifold/piping level, free-cooling (outside-air) integration, and finally achieving PUE ≤ 1.15 alongside infrastructure reliability.

Subsection 2.3.1 makes the case in two parts. First, the surge in AI GPU power density: rack density has risen 3–5× over five years, with NVIDIA Blackwell (B200/B300) pushing single servers past 15kW and six-server racks past 90kW. A comparison table (Table 2-4) traces per-generation server power and rack density — A100 (6.5kW, 13–39kW, air-coolable), H100 (10.2kW, 20–61kW, entering air-cooling limits), H200 (11.0kW, 22–66kW, transitional), B200 (14.3kW, 29–86kW, D2C under consideration), and B300 (~15kW, 30–90kW, D2C mandatory). The text argues this is structural rather than temporary — Moore's Law slowdown pushes vendors toward parallel-compute density, so thermal density rises with it — and concludes that data center infrastructure should be designed forward-compatible through the B300 generation rather than to current-generation requirements.

Second, the thermodynamic limit of air cooling: air's volumetric heat capacity (1.2 kJ/m³·°C) is roughly 3,500× lower than water's (4,186 kJ/m³·°C), so removing the same heat load requires ~3,500× the flow volume, driving transport power up exponentially. Past roughly 10kW per server, fan power exceeds 15% of IT load, producing the paradox of cooling fans themselves inflating server power consumption.

This partial document is section 2.3 (전력 및 냉각 설계) of a data-center system architecture guide, covering why air cooling has run out of headroom for AI racks and why Direct-to-Chip (D2C) liquid cooling is now mandatory.

Main points covered:

- **Section framing (2.3)** — as per-rack AI accelerator density passes 60kW, air cooling hits thermodynamic, physical, operational, and energy-efficiency limits simultaneously; the section promises to cover D2C mechanisms, water-cooling validation requirements, CDU/manifold/piping design parameters, free-cooling integration, PUE ≤ 1.15, and infrastructure reliability.

- **2.3.1 Limits of air cooling**
  - *GPU power density surge*: rack density up 3–5× in five years; a generation-by-generation table (Table 2-4) of 8-GPU server power and rack density — A100 6.5kW/13–39kW, H100 10.2kW/20–61kW, H200 11.0kW/22–66kW, B200 14.3kW/29–86kW, B300 ~15kW/30–90kW — with D2C shifting from "consider" to "required." Argues this is structural (Moore's Law slowdown → density-driven performance), so infrastructure must be designed forward-compatible to B300.
  - *Thermodynamic limit*: air's volumetric heat capacity (1.2 kJ/m³·°C) is ~3,500× lower than water's (4,186), requiring ~3,500× the flow; above 10kW/server, fan power exceeds 15% of IT load — cooling fans paradoxically inflate server power draw. Table 2-5 compares specific heat, volumetric heat capacity, and heat transfer coefficients for air, water, and 25% propylene-glycol mix (the PG mix noted as used for water-quality/corrosion/fouling control in D2C loops, not just antifreeze).
  - *Per-technology ceilings* (Table 2-6): CRAC/CRAH ~20kW/rack, containment and in-row ~30kW, rear-door HX (indirect liquid) ~50kW, D2C and immersion 30–150+kW/rack — above 75kW/rack only direct liquid cooling works.
  - *ASHRAE standards*: TC 9.9 5th Ed. (2021) A1–A4 classes plus the new H1 class for high-density gear with a stricter 25°C recommended inlet cap (higher density → narrower allowable range); 2024's shift from Datacom Series to Datacom Encyclopedia adding the S Class for liquid cooling supply temperature, formalizing the industry's pivot from air-optimized to liquid-based design. Table 2-7 maps classes to inlet temperature ranges, power density, and cooling method.
  - *Supporting evidence and practical failure modes*: Almoli et al. (2012) CFD work showing >8°C inlet temperature non-uniformity above 20kW/rack even with cold-aisle containment; at high density, air cooling brings large CRAC footprint growth, uncontrollable high-volume airflow (dust ingress, condensate carryover), and 80–95 dBA noise plus vibration from maxed fan RPM.
  - *Climate and PUE*: Seoul 50-year extreme conditions (39.0°C summer / −21.1°C winter) per ASHRAE Climatic Design Conditions 2025 make peak chiller load prohibitive for air cooling, while D2C pushes free-cooling availability above 90%. Table 2-8 compares annual Seoul PUE — air 1.60–1.80, air with free cooling 1.35–1.50 (~70% availability), D2C with free cooling 1.10–1.30 (~90%+) — with a footnote documenting the BIN-data methodology (8,760 h, ~6,132 h vs ~7,884 h of free-cooling hours at 15°C vs 25°C outdoor dry-bulb thresholds under W3/W4 warm-water design).

- **2.3.2 D2C liquid cooling infrastructure (beginning)** — mechanism: cold plates clamped directly to CPU/GPU dies with microchannel coolant flow, removing heat by conduction with no air in the path, yielding heat transfer coefficients tens of times higher and enabling 75kW+/rack (referencing NHN FactoryX). Table 2-9 compares heat-removal paths and loop counts: air-cooled with chiller (4 stages), D2C with chiller (4 stages), and D2C with cooling tower only (3 stages). Key argument: the stage count matters less than the presence of an air-mediated stage — the heatsink→air segment has a very low heat transfer coefficient (25–250 W/m²K) and accounts for 60–70% of total thermal resistance, which D2C eliminates entirely; the chiller-less cooling-tower variant is tied to ASHRAE W4 class operation.

nodes.title: D2C 수랭식 인프라 도입
nodes.summary:
This section documents the transition from air cooling to Direct-to-Chip (D2C) liquid cooling in NHN FactoryX's AI data center architecture, covering three main areas:

**Cooling efficiency comparison and D2C mechanism** — A PUE comparison table (Seoul-based annual estimates) shows air cooling at 1.60–1.80, air cooling with free cooling at 1.35–1.50 (~70% free-cooling availability), and D2C liquid cooling at 1.10–1.30 (~90%+ availability), with methodology footnoted from KMA 1991–2020 climate normals and ASHRAE 2025 extreme conditions. D2C mounts cold plates directly on CPU/GPU packages, achieving heat transfer coefficients tens of times higher than air. A heat-removal path table compares air-cooled (4 stages), D2C with chiller (4 stages), and D2C with cooling tower only (3 stages) — the key distinction being elimination of the air-mediated stage, which alone accounts for 60–70% of total thermal resistance. The chiller-free cooling tower configuration (ASHRAE W4, supply ≤45°C) yields the best PUE but requires wet-bulb temperature validation for Korean summers. The document argues air cooling has hit simultaneous thermodynamic, operational, and energy-efficiency limits, making D2C an engineering necessity above 75kW/rack.

**Five verification requirements before liquid-cooling adoption** — vendor compatibility (cold plate mounting specs, OEM warranty risk), interface standardization (CDU vendor lock-in, ongoing OCP/ASHRAE TC 9.9/ISO work on QD connector specs), operational parameter validation (supply/return temperature, flow rate, pressure; commissioning under real IT load with design-vs-measured deviation analysis), scalability (H100→B200→B300 transitions raising rack power 30–40%), and coolant quality management (resistivity, pH, metal ions, biofilm; NHN's choice of 25% propylene glycol requiring higher-head pumps).

**Liquid-cooling component design** — CDU design criteria table (ASHRAE W20~W+ supply temperature, ~70% of IT load handled by liquid with the remaining 30% air-cooled, OCP-recommended ≤2.0 bar rack pressure drop, resistivity and pH standards), sized against NHN's 75kW/rack load. Manifold and QD connector selection emphasizes parallel supply/return separation for fast, leak-free server swaps given short GPU refresh cycles and cluster-wide impact of single-node failures. Free-cooling operation uses three modes based on outdoor conditions against a 20°C coolant supply temperature; with ~80% of the year below 26°C outdoor temperature, PUE 1.15 is achievable.

nodes.title: 수랭식 시스템 요소 설계
nodes.summary:
This section documents the water-cooling (D2C liquid cooling) system architecture for NHN FactoryX, covering:

**Water quality management** — Risks of skipping regular monitoring of ion concentration and microbial standards (corrosion, scale, biofilm clogging flow paths and raising cold-plate thermal resistance). FactoryX uses a PG 25% water mixture, with a high-head pump selected to account for the mixture's higher viscosity.

**CDU design criteria (Table 2-10)** — Chilled water supplied via a chiller to keep GPU temperatures low. Water cooling handles the cold-plate-mounted CPU/GPU load (~70% of server rated load), while memory, power supplies, and mainboard remain air-cooled (~30%). Applied to a 75kW/rack load. Criteria follow ASHRAE and OCP standards: supply temperature ASHRAE W20~W+, allowable in-rack pressure drop ≤2.0 bar per OCP, plus resistivity (corrosion prevention) and pH per OCP water-quality standards.

**Manifold and QD connector design** — Manifolds distribute and return chilled water to GPU servers in the rack; Quick Disconnect couplers allow leak-free connection/separation. Because AI servers have short replacement cycles across GPU generations and a single server failure can affect an entire cluster's training job, supply/return piping is designed for parallel isolation.

**Free-cooling operation (Table 2-11)** — Three operating modes based on outdoor air conditions for the 20°C chilled water supply, based on 2025 KMA Seoul weather data: free cooling ≤18°C (5,024 h, 57.4%, chiller off/heat exchanger on), partial free cooling 18–26°C (2,150 h, 24.5%, both on), and chiller operation >26°C (1,586 h, 18.1%). About 80% of the year is at or below 26°C, enabling PUE 1.15.

**PUE improvement and infrastructure reliability** — D2C dissipates heat directly at the GPU chip; under ASHRAE W27 with outdoor-air cooling, PUE ≤1.15 is realistic, cutting annual cooling energy ~30–40% versus air cooling (PUE 1.6–1.8). Reliability measures include precise chip-temperature control to lower failure rates, dry-break QDs, N+1 CDU pumps, and leak-sensor integration. Interface standardization and extensibility allow reuse of existing cooling infrastructure across next-generation GPU platforms, and the smaller footprint yields ~75% fewer racks versus 20kW/rack air cooling at equal IT capacity.

nodes.title: PUE 개선 및 인프라 신뢰성 확보
nodes.summary:
This section covers data center cooling operations and efficiency outcomes for NHN FactoryX's D2C (Direct-to-Chip) liquid cooling system.

**Free-cooling operating criteria (Table 2-11):** Three operating modes keyed to outdoor air temperature — full pre-cooling at ≤18°C (5,024 h/yr, 57.4%, chiller OFF with pre-cooling heat exchanger ON), partial pre-cooling at 18–26°C (2,150 h, 24.5%, both chiller and heat exchanger ON), and chiller-only operation above 26°C (1,586 h, 18.1%).

**PUE improvement:** By dissipating GPU chip heat directly, the D2C system fundamentally reduces cooling energy. Under ASHRAE W27 conditions combined with outdoor-air cooling, a PUE of ≤1.15 is deemed realistically achievable — roughly 30–40% annual cooling energy savings versus air-cooled systems (PUE 1.6–1.8).

**Infrastructure reliability:** Precise GPU temperature control lowers failure rates from overheating and improves server availability. Risk is mitigated through dry-break quick disconnects (QD), N+1 CDU pump redundancy, and leak-sensor integration. Standardized interfaces and scalability allow the existing cooling infrastructure to be reused across next-generation GPU platforms, while the smaller footprint per IT capacity yields about a 75% reduction in rack count versus 20kW/rack air cooling.

nodes.title: GPU 동적 할당 기술(GPU Live)
nodes.summary:
This document section covers GPU dynamic allocation technology (GPU Live) within a system architecture document, presented as Section 2.4.

It opens by framing the core challenge of large-scale GPU cluster operation — optimally distributing limited high-performance compute resources across many users and heterogeneous workloads — and identifies three characteristics that distinguish GPU clusters from traditional CPU-centric ones: high resource unit cost where low utilization translates directly into major operating losses; workload heterogeneity across training, inference, and data preprocessing that makes a single policy unworkable; and scaling complexity spanning everything from large-scale distributed training beyond a single GPU to fine-grained fractional allocation of one GPU. From these it argues that conventional cloud resource management models cannot be applied as-is, motivating GPU-specialized allocation and scheduling, and states the section's aim of defining the concept and describing how NHN FactoryX's GPU Live integrates it within a standard Kubernetes environment.

Subsection 2.4.1 then contrasts static and dynamic allocation. Static allocation assigns GPUs fixed to teams or projects — simple to operate and predictable for users, but structurally unable to redistribute idle resources; debugging/idle periods in training, low-traffic windows for inference, and differing departmental usage patterns leave many GPUs idle, a cluster-level allocation/busy utilization concern distinct from in-job efficiency metrics like MFU, with trace analyses reportedly showing utilization ranging from single digits to around 30% depending on workload mix. Dynamic allocation instead manages GPUs as a shared pool with on-demand assignment and reclamation, raising utilization but introducing three operational burdens: scheduling complexity (priority, resource fit, and topology considered together in placement decisions), policy consistency (simultaneously satisfying per-user/team/project quotas and guarantees), and fault resilience (keeping running workloads stable while resources are dynamically reclaimed and reassigned). The subsection is also introduced as covering resource sharing and scaling plus the underlying scheduling and policy models.

nodes.title: GPU 동적 할당 기술의 개념과 필요성
nodes.summary:
This section covers GPU dynamic allocation technology (GPU Live) within a system architecture document, structured in two parts.

**2.4.1 — Concepts and rationale for dynamic GPU allocation**

It opens by framing why GPU clusters differ from CPU-centric ones: high unit cost (so low utilization directly means wasted spend), workload heterogeneity (training, inference, preprocessing each need different GPU usage patterns), and scaling complexity (from multi-node distributed training down to fractions of a single GPU).

- **Static vs. dynamic allocation** — Static allocation fixes GPUs per team/project; simple and predictable but leaves idle resources unrecoverable, with cited cluster trace analyses showing allocation/busy utilization ranging from single digits to ~30%. Dynamic allocation pools GPUs and assigns on demand, raising utilization at the cost of scheduling complexity, policy consistency, and fault resilience.
- **GPU sharing (splitting one GPU)** — Compares four methods: time-slicing (NVIDIA Device Plugin, no isolation, suited to dev/experiment/education), MPS (spatial SM sharing across CUDA contexts, lower context-switch overhead, still no memory/fault isolation, fits single-trust-boundary inference/HPC), MIG (hardware-level partitioning up to 7 instances on A100/H100-class GPUs, strong isolation for multi-tenancy, but fixed profiles and reconfiguration requiring workload termination), and vGPU (hypervisor-level, requires paid NVIDIA licensing). Table 2-12 compares them across isolation level, supported GPUs, partition unit, runtime reconfiguration, license cost, and suitable workloads.
- **GPU scaling (combining GPUs)** — Multi-GPU scale-up via NVLink/NVSwitch with per-GPU bidirectional bandwidth figures (600GB/s on A100, 900GB/s on H100/H200, 1.8TB/s on Blackwell) and sub-microsecond latency for tensor/model parallelism; multi-node scale-out over InfiniBand/RoCE with NCCL collectives, requiring gang scheduling (via Coscheduling/Volcano, since the default Kubernetes scheduler is per-Pod) and topology-aware placement.
- **Bin packing against fragmentation** — Explains how repeated workload churn leaves enough aggregate GPUs but not N contiguous on one node, and covers first-fit, best-fit, and worst-fit variants, noting real schedulers generalize these into weighted scoring functions.
- **Resource management policy model** — Four interlocking elements drawn from Borg/YARN practice: quota, guaranteed quota, overcommit/overbooking, and reclaim (illustrated in Figure 2-1), plus priority and preemption for contention. A worked conflict scenario walks through a 100-GPU cluster with 60-GPU quotas for projects A and B (1.2x overbooking) and a 40-GPU guarantee for A, showing how the policies resolve simultaneous demand spikes.

**2.4.2 — GPU Live's dynamic allocation implementation**

Introduces GPU Live as NHN FactoryX's resource management layer that abstracts GPUs into a single pool and runs the above model on Kubernetes, handling resource pooling, policy enforcement, and lifecycle management with a self-service user experience — built on proven standard Kubernetes components (Device Plugin, Topology Manager, etc.) rather than a custom scheduler or cluster manager.

nodes.title: GPU Live의 동적 할당 기술
nodes.summary:
This section of the document covers the system architecture of GPU resource management, moving from general dynamic-allocation theory to NHN FactoryX's GPU Live implementation.

**Resource management policy model (four elements):** It explains how quota, guaranteed allocation, overbooking, and reclamation interact, and how contention among them is resolved through priority and preemption — reclamation recovers idle resources, while preemption forcibly terminates lower-priority active workloads to meet guaranteed quotas or time-sensitive SLAs. Comparable mechanisms in Borg (production vs. batch tiers), YARN Capacity Scheduler (inter-queue preemption), and Kubernetes (PriorityClass/Preemption) are cited. A worked conflict scenario illustrates the model: 100 physical GPUs, 60-GPU quotas issued to each of two projects (1.2 overbooking ratio), with Project A holding a 40-GPU guarantee — showing how reclamation and preemption resolve simultaneous demand spikes and how excess workloads get queued.

**GPU Live's dynamic allocation technology (2.4.2):**
- *Kubernetes-standard integration* — building on proven OSS components (Device Plugin, Topology Manager, GPU-aware schedulers) rather than a custom scheduler, yielding standardization, operational validation, and extensibility to future accelerators such as NPUs. The differentiator is claimed to be integration and operating policy, not component choice.
- *Three-tier multi-tenancy* — System → Organization → Project layers, with resource isolation via per-layer GPU quotas (project quota validated at workload creation, usage aggregated to the organization), hierarchical policy inheritance with lower-level override, and RBAC-based access isolation mapping each project to a Kubernetes namespace.
- *Dynamic allocation model and lifecycle* — GPUs pooled rather than fixed per node; allocation granularity ranges from a single GPU to multi-node/multi-GPU, supporting Multi-GPU scale-up and Multi-Node scale-out over InfiniBand-class interconnects.
- *Training vs. inference lifecycle differences* — training has defined start/end, gang-scheduled batch start/stop with immediate reclamation and whole-job restart on worker failure; inference runs as a long-lived service with per-instance GPU sets, per-instance recovery/relocation, and quota re-validation plus bin-packing on relocation, with autoscaling handled by standard Kubernetes mechanisms.
- *Multi-node scheduling* — gang scheduling holds the entire job in queue unless all workers are simultaneously available, preventing partial-start waste and synchronization deadlock.
- *Bin-packing* — GPU-first best-fit placement onto already-occupied nodes, minimizing node-level fragmentation and preserving empty nodes as contiguous capacity for large distributed training jobs.
- *Resource management status* — GPU Live currently operates quota-based scheduling, overbooking, and automatic idle reclamation (immediate on normal termination, threshold-based for idle workloads, forced on project expiry or policy violation); guaranteed allocation is not yet applied and is deferred to a future phase. A five-step operational conflict procedure is given for the >90% utilization case: quota check → capacity search → reclaimable candidate selection → reclaim and schedule (reclaimed workloads return to queue) → automated execution with operator-visible monitoring.

The excerpt ends by opening section 2.4.3 (Future Development Directions, as of June 2026), summarizing that dynamic allocation overcomes static allocation's utilization limits through GPU partitioning, GPU aggregation, bin-packing, and the four-element resource management model.

nodes.title: 향후 개발 방향
nodes.summary:
This partial document covers the resource-management portion of a GPU infrastructure system architecture chapter (section 2.4.x, "시스템 아키텍처"), focusing on GPU Live's dynamic allocation model and its future roadmap.

**Main points:**

1. **Quota-based scheduling** — GPU quotas defined at two tiers (organization and project); project quota is validated at workload creation to block over-limit requests. Organization quota currently serves as a usage-tracking/policy unit, with hard enforcement to be strengthened alongside guaranteed allocation.

2. **Overbooking** — Issuing total user quota in excess of physical GPU capacity to raise cluster utilization, relying on the statistical fact that users rarely hit their limits simultaneously, combined with reclamation to resolve contention under high load.

3. **Automatic idle-resource reclamation** — Three triggers: immediate reclaim on normal workload termination, policy-based reclaim of workloads below a GPU-usage threshold for a sustained period, and forced reclaim on project expiry or resource-policy violation. Reclaimed resources return to the pool immediately.

4. **Operational conflict scenario** — A five-step walkthrough of what happens when cluster GPU utilization exceeds 90% and a new workload is requested: quota check → available-resource search → selection of "reclaimable" candidates (idle or low-priority workloads) → reclaim, schedule the new workload, and return the reclaimed one to the queue → all automatic, with reclaim/re-placement history traceable via monitoring tools. Quantitative per-user/project SLA guarantees are noted as a later phase.

5. **Section summary (2.4.3 향후 개발 방향, as of June 2026)** — Dynamic allocation in general comprises GPU partitioning, GPU aggregation, bin packing, and the four-element resource model (quota, guaranteed allocation, overbooking, reclamation); GPU Live integrates these on standard Kubernetes with 3-tier multi-tenancy (System/Organization/Project), GPU-first bin packing, and differentiated training/inference lifecycles.

6. **Kubernetes standards evolution** — Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA), GA in Kubernetes 1.34, is positioned as the successor to the Device Plugin model (structured resource model, topology awareness, MIG, heterogeneous accelerators); NVIDIA/AMD/Intel are migrating to DRA drivers, and GPU Live will keep its current Device Plugin operation while evaluating DRA adoption in stages.

7. **Roadmap** — Feature-side: MIG spatial partitioning, NUMA affinity and multi-node topology-aware placement, refined training/inference co-location policy, and guaranteed allocation for SLA assurance. Scope-side: extending the same model to NPUs and other heterogeneous accelerators, applying it first to inference workloads (given domestic NPUs' inference specialization) and later to training; device recognition/allocation infrastructure is already in production while scheduling and resource-policy integration proceeds in phases.

8. **Ends with the table of contents for the next chapter, "03 하드웨어 구성"** (3.1 CPU and memory, 3.2 GPU specs and performance, 3.3 storage and network).

structure.title: 03 하드웨어 구성
structure.summary:
This section covers hardware configuration for AI/GPU clusters, framed around the principle that the cluster should be designed as a balanced whole system rather than as a sum of individual node specs, using NHN FactoryX's standard GPU node reference configuration as the basis.

The main focus is CPU and memory design (§3.1). It explains that in AI workloads the CPU's role is not computation but feeding data to the GPU without interruption — insufficient CPU leaves GPUs idle waiting on data, commonly dropping GPU utilization below 60%. Three design principles follow:

- **PCIe Gen5 lane provisioning** — GPUs, NICs, and NVMe all demand PCIe Gen5 x16, so CPUs must supply enough lanes per socket.
- **NUMA-aware design** — standardizing slot placement so GPU, NIC, and NVMe align to the same NUMA node, reducing cross-socket interconnect traffic and stabilizing per-training-step data loading latency.
- **System-to-GPU memory ratio** — system memory should be at least 2× the node's total GPU memory, to accommodate data prefetch, optimizer state offloading, checkpoint staging buffers, and distributed-training communication buffers.

It closes with a recommended configuration table (Table 3-1): dual-socket Intel Xeon Scalable (Sapphire Rapids/Emerald Rapids) or AMD EPYC (Genoa/Bergamo), example core count of 2×56C = 112C, 2TB DDR5 ECC RDIMM per node (1TB–4TB range), 8+ memory channels per socket in a NUMA-aware full-channel layout, and PCIe Gen5 with adequate x16 lane distribution across GPU/NIC/NVMe slots.

nodes.title: GPU 사양 및 성능
nodes.summary:
This section covers GPU hardware specifications within NHN FactoryX's infrastructure. It explains that AI workloads have divergent GPU requirements by stage — pre-training demands large HBM capacity, high BF16/FP8 throughput, and wide inter-node bandwidth, while inference and fine-tuning are governed more by response latency and cost per token when serving a single model to many users. Because assigning identical GPUs to all workloads is inefficient in cost and power terms, NHN FactoryX separates its fleet into a high-performance training GPU line and an inference/fine-tuning GPU line.

The bulk of the section is a comparison table (표 3-2) of NVIDIA GPU generations — A100 SXM, H100 SXM, H200 SXM, B200 SXM, and B300 SXM — across architecture (Ampere, Hopper, Blackwell, Blackwell Ultra), HBM capacity per GPU (80GB → 270GB), HBM bandwidth (2TB/s → 7.7TB/s), tensor throughput at FP64/TF32/BF16-FP16/FP8/FP4 precisions, NVLink bandwidth (600GB/s → 1,800GB/s), and TDP (400W → 1,400W). It also notes each generation's primary compute precision and representative workload, tracing the progression from general-purpose AI training (A100), through scientific computing and LLM training (H100/H200) and large-model inference, to LLM training/inference on B200 and dedicated LLM inference service on B300 — highlighting the trend of declining FP64 capability alongside the introduction of FP8 and FP4 support in newer generations.

nodes.title: 스토리지 및 네트워크
nodes.summary:
This section (3.3 of a hardware configuration document) covers storage and network design for AI training/inference infrastructure, framing both as paired data paths that must keep pace with GPU throughput or cluster utilization suffers.

**3.3.1 Tiered Storage** — Presents a three-tier structure (Table 3-3) separating workloads by I/O characteristics for cost/performance optimization:
- Tier 0: node-local NVMe for data loader cache and checkpoint staging, requiring GPUDirect Storage support
- Tier 1: parallel file systems (Lustre/GPFS/WekaFS) for active training datasets, requiring multi-client concurrent throughput and metadata performance
- Tier 2: object storage for source datasets, archives, and cold checkpoints, prioritizing capacity, durability, and cost efficiency

It explains the data lifecycle flow across tiers — source data held in Tier 2, active datasets prefetched to Tier 1, mini-batches staged in Tier 0 NVMe closest to the GPU — and the reverse flow for checkpoints (frequent temporary checkpoints written to Tier 0, permanent copies asynchronously replicated to Tier 2), keeping only hot data near GPUs.

**3.3.2 Network Configuration** — Describes physically separating three fabrics plus a dedicated out-of-band plane, each independently tuned so traffic types don't interfere:
- Compute Fabric: InfiniBand NDR 400Gbps × 8 NICs per node (rail-optimized)
- Storage Fabric: 100/200/400GbE or a separate InfiniBand plane with GPUDirect Storage enabled
- Management/In-band Fabric: redundant 10/25GbE for orchestration, monitoring, and image deployment
- Out-of-band Management: separate 1GbE plane for BMC/IPMI, ensuring power and console control independent of compute-plane failures

structure.title: 04 성능 분석
structure.summary:
This document section covers **performance analysis of a GPU cluster (Chapter 4)**, with these main points:

**Two-axis evaluation framework** — Performance must be assessed both as theoretical compute capacity based on official hardware specs, and as effective performance actually achieved in real distributed training/inference workloads. A gap between these two values almost always exists, and the size of that gap defines the cluster's true operational efficiency.

**Chapter roadmap** — The chapter proceeds from (1) how theoretical compute performance is calculated, to (2) five degradation patterns that create the gap between theoretical and measured values, along with each pattern's measurement metrics and remediation direction, and closes with (3) a checklist of items to verify at the design stage rather than during operations.

**4.1 Theoretical compute performance** — Introduces the formula: Cluster Peak FLOPS = (number of nodes) × (GPUs per node) × (per-GPU peak FLOPS). Worked example: 32 nodes × 8 H100 SXM GPUs × 3,958 TFLOPS ≈ 1.01 ExaFLOPS (FP8 Sparse, theoretical).

**MFU (Model FLOPS Utilization)** — This theoretical figure is an upper bound; real training workloads typically reach only 40–60% of it. MFU is the efficiency metric capturing all GPU idle time from communication, data waits, checkpointing, etc. Well-designed LLM training clusters target 50%+ MFU; falling short signals that one or more of the five degradation patterns (covered in section 4.2) is accumulating.

nodes.title: 성능 저하 패턴 분석
nodes.summary:
This section covers performance degradation pattern analysis in large-scale GPU training, presenting three of five common patterns that explain gaps between theoretical and measured performance — each with its own symptoms, root causes, and diagnostic metrics:

**1. Communication-bound (network bottleneck)** — GPUs idle while inter-node communication lags. Symptoms: low SM activity, below-normal GPU power draw, periodic burst patterns in NIC traffic, and All-Reduce consuming over 30% of total step time. Causes range from oversubscribed topology or rail-alignment failure, to insufficient per-NIC bandwidth, to untuned NCCL environment variables. Diagnose via NCCL all_reduce time, SM Activity vs. DRAM Active ratio, and NIC RX/TX vs. GPU FLOPS ratio.

**2. Memory shortage (HBM/system memory)** — Surfaces as OOM errors, or as slowdowns from forcibly shrinking micro-batches to avoid OOM. Under heavier pressure, activation recomputation is used (discarding intermediate values and recomputing on demand to save memory, at the cost of speed). Root cause: parameters + optimizer states + activations exceeding HBM capacity, or insufficient system memory causing page-fault thrashing. Diagnose via peak GPU memory occupancy, OOM frequency, and activation-recomputation application rate.

**3. Storage I/O bottleneck** — GPU utilization drops near zero from epoch start and never recovers, with data loader workers stuck waiting. Four typical causes: insufficient storage throughput, metadata overhead from too many small files, GPUDirect Storage disabled (forcing the slow CPU-mediated path), and too few loader workers — often two or more occurring together in practice. Diagnose via data-loader wait time as a fraction of step time, storage throughput (GB/s), and metadata operations per second, to distinguish throughput-driven from metadata-driven bottlenecks.

nodes.summary:
This partial document covers sections 4.2.4–4.2.5 of a performance analysis chapter on GPU cluster training bottlenecks, in Korean.

**4.2.4 Thermal Throttling** — Describes the symptom (GPU clocks stepping down over long training runs, with per-step times gradually increasing), the causes (insufficient rack-level cooling capacity, poor hot/cold aisle containment, uneven HVAC airflow, and failure to anticipate the heat load of running the whole cluster at full load), and the diagnostic approach (comparing GPU temperature distribution by rack/node/socket, clock-throttling event rates, and throughput variance across nodes running the same workload to locate where thermal limits accumulate).

nodes.title: 패턴별 설계 단계 대응 체크리스트
nodes.summary:
This partial document covers the tail end of a performance-analysis chapter (Section 4.3) and the start of a scalability/operations chapter (Section 5).

**Main points:**

- **Rationale for design-time prevention** — Once these degradation patterns surface in production, training cost and schedule have already been impacted, and remediation requires expensive measures like halting workloads or reconfiguring the cluster. The checklist is therefore framed as design-stage verification items that map 1:1 to the five patterns introduced in Section 4.2.

- **Table 4-1: Design-stage checklist by degradation pattern**
  - *Network bottleneck* — verify 1:1 non-blocking Leaf-Spine, rail-optimized cabling, NIC bandwidth per GPU (≥100 Gbps/GPU recommended), SHARP and Adaptive Routing enablement, and pre-validation of NCCL topology.
  - *Memory shortage* — pre-calculate the memory footprint for target model and sequence length, size system memory at ≥2× total GPU memory, and assess applicability of optimizer-state sharding (ZeRO/FSDP).
  - *Storage I/O* — define a sustained read-bandwidth KPI per GPU (e.g., 2 GB/s/GPU), use a GPUDirect Storage–capable filesystem, and consolidate small files via sharding/archive formats such as WebDataset.
  - *Thermal throttling* — pre-compute per-rack heat load (kW), enforce hot/cold aisle containment, simulate simultaneous full-load scenarios during node placement, and install temperature sensors at top/middle/bottom of racks.
  - *Checkpoint overhead* — adopt asynchronous/distributed checkpointing (e.g., DCP), reserve dedicated checkpoint storage bandwidth, and set checkpoint intervals from an RPO-based analysis of loss cost.

- **Transition to Chapter 5 (Scalability and Operations)** — introduces upcoming sections on scale-out strategy (5.1) and resource utilization efficiency (5.2).

structure.title: 05 확장성 및 운영
structure.summary:
This section (Chapter 05) covers scalability and operations for NHN FactoryX's GPU infrastructure, framing infrastructure value in terms of post-deployment TCO and usability rather than initial build-out — specifically expansion cost as workloads change, how operational burden grows as resources are added, and actual GPU asset utilization.

Section 5.1 details the scale-out strategy, arguing that cluster expansion is more than adding GPUs: new resources must be absorbed into existing workload performance and automation coverage at the same level, without halting operations or requiring major changes.

- **5.1.1 Scalable Unit-based expansion**: A predefined Scalable Unit is the minimum increment, bundling N standard-configuration GPU nodes, a Rail-Optimized Leaf switch group, storage client licenses and bandwidth allocation, and management-plane IP/DNS/certificate auto-issuance resources. This standardization delivers two benefits — predictable performance and cost per increment, and operational automation (IaC, image deployment, health checks) applying identically to new units so operational burden does not grow proportionally.

- **5.1.2 Separating horizontal from vertical scaling**: Scaling direction is chosen by the nature of the resource the workload demands, distinguishing "handling more jobs" from "running one job bigger." Scale-out applies when the number of concurrent workloads and total compute grows (ultra-large model training, multi-tenant environments), handled via Scalable Unit increments. Scale-up applies when a single model lacks memory or bandwidth, handled by expanding the NVLink domain (e.g. NVL72) or adopting next-generation GPUs to raise the per-node resource ceiling.

structure.title: 06 활용 사례
structure.summary:
This section (Chapter 6, "활용 사례") introduces two case studies showing how the previously discussed infrastructure design and operations principles are realized in production services: (1) a multi-tenant GPUaaS environment where multiple companies/organizations share the same infrastructure, and (2) an enterprise private AI infrastructure where a single company runs a dedicated cluster in GPUaaS form. Though the two differ in resource-isolation and operational-automation requirements, both are built on the same GPUaaS platform architecture, demonstrating the extensibility of NHN FactoryX's operating model.

Section 6.1 covers NHN FactoryX's exascale cluster. It first contrasts delivery models: bare-metal allocation assigns GPU resources per physical server, letting users fully configure their runtime environment and maximize hardware performance, but because node-level admin privileges go directly to users, tenant-to-tenant security isolation is not guaranteed in shared infrastructure, and divergent per-tenant environments make consistent infrastructure-level operational policy hard to apply during incidents.

To overcome this, the NHN FactoryX Seoul data center layers a GPUaaS platform on top of a GPU infrastructure of 957 GPU nodes. The platform integrates management of the scheduling system and container environment, and applies resource/security control consistently across infrastructure through a hierarchical Tenant → Workspace → Project structure: operators separate users by tenant, create projects and workspaces under each tenant, logically cap each tenant's available compute, and restrict users to resources within their own tenant.

Figure 6-1 illustrates a multi-tenant GPUaaS configuration example — a cluster of 255 B200 units, with Tenant A holding GPU Nodes 1–4 plus 40T storage and Tenant B holding GPU Nodes 5–6 plus 20T storage.

nodes.title: NHN FactoryX: 엑사스케일 클러스터

The main focus is **6.1 NHN FactoryX: Exascale Cluster**, which covers:

- **Bare-metal vs. GPUaaS trade-offs** — bare metal assigns GPU resources per physical server and maximizes hardware performance, but granting node-level admin rights to users breaks tenant security isolation and makes consistent infrastructure-wide operational policy hard to apply during failures.
- **Platform architecture** — NHN FactoryX's Seoul data center layers a GPUaaS platform on top of 957 GPU nodes, integrating scheduling systems and container environments.
- **Hierarchical resource/security control** — a Tenant → Workspace → Project structure, where operators segment users by tenant, compute resources are logically capped per tenant, and users can only consume resources within their own tenant (illustrated in Figure 6-1, showing tenants A and B with separate GPU nodes and storage quotas on a 255-node B200 cluster).
- **Performance validation** — addressing concerns that the added service layer causes network bottlenecks and degrades training performance; containers retain host-level network performance, and a 255-node HPL (High Performance Linpack) benchmark on the GPUaaS platform achieved parity with bare metal.
- **Operational status as of June 2026** — clusters 1 and 2 serve industry, academic, and research organizations across 510- and 255-node GPUaaS deployments, each in isolated workspaces. Examples include institution A (multimodal AI and LLM multi-agent research for healthcare applications) and institution B (proprietary LLM training and service experimentation).
- **Fault isolation** — a failure or resource-usage spike in tenant A's workspace does not affect tenant B's training or services, since each operates on independently separated resources and networks.

The section concludes that the Seoul data center satisfies both cross-organization security isolation and resource control requirements on a single platform, enabling many users to stably share the same GPU infrastructure, with continued operational improvements planned.

**Main points:**

- **Problem framing** — Companies pursuing company-wide AI strategy face heavy time and cost burdens when building their own GPU infrastructure (data center design, power/cooling, GPU procurement, operations staffing, network fabric tuning). Workload characteristics vary by department/business unit, making it hard to achieve both resource allocation and operational isolation on a single infrastructure. Generic public-cloud GPU instances reduce the procurement burden but cannot guarantee dedicated-cluster-level performance and isolation, and limit flexible application of company-specific security and operations policies.

- **NHN Cloud's solution** — Instead of building their own data centers and GPU/network resources, enterprises are allocated a standardized, dedicated GPU cluster with the GPUaaS platform layered on top — reducing build time/cost while securing dedicated-cluster performance and security isolation.

- **Cluster 3 case study** — A 192-GPU-node cluster shared independently by two companies: Company E (gaming industry) uses ~40 nodes for AI model development and operations; Company F (AI industry) uses ~140 nodes for LLM training.

- **How isolation works** — The GPUaaS platform's tenant isolation architecture lets each company and its internal departments receive resources as independent tenants, developing and operating LLM, multimodal, and conversational AI models via a web-based management console without cross-tenant interference. Each company's infrastructure administrators use the same web platform to monitor all nodes' resource status centrally and unify department-level resource allocation and access-permission management.

- **Significance and closing** — The model reduces self-build burden while simultaneously satisfying inter-department independent operation and integrated management, with plans for continued flexible scaling and operational efficiency improvements. The chapter concludes by noting that both cases — despite differing resource-isolation units and operating entities — are implemented on the same GPUaaS platform architecture, demonstrating that NHN FactoryX's operating model can accommodate diverse AI workload requirements across academia, research, and industry under a single infrastructure standard. structure.title: 07 결론
structure.summary:
This partial document contains the conclusion (Chapter 7) and the appendix table of contents (Chapter 8) of a technical white paper on NHN FactoryX's AI-dedicated infrastructure.

**Main points covered:**

**Framing of the problem** — Generative AI and LLMs have pushed enterprise compute scale beyond what general-purpose cloud infrastructure was designed for. Four structural bottlenecks are named: communication/overhead, data starvation, checkpoint-write bottlenecks, and surging power density. The argument is that these cannot be solved by hardware improvements alone and require an AI-dedicated infrastructure integrated across every layer, from physical facilities to the software management tier.

**Recap of Chapter 2 (System Architecture)** — A Scalable Unit–based four-tier cluster structure; physical separation of the Compute, Storage, and Management fabrics to eliminate traffic interference; Fat-Tree Rail-Optimized topology to minimize collective-communication end-to-end latency; NVSwitch Full-Mesh for uniform intra-node GPU bandwidth; InfiniBand RDMA, Adaptive Routing, and SHARP for inter-node communication. Power and cooling use D2C liquid cooling that removes air-mediated stages entirely, with free-cooling integration expected to achieve PUE ≤ 1.15. GPU Live abstracts GPUs into a single pool on standard Kubernetes, combining three-tier multi-tenancy, bin packing, quotas, overbooking, and automatic reclamation to overcome static-allocation utilization limits.

**Recap of Chapter 3 (Hardware Configuration)** — Balanced CPU/memory ratios to keep GPUs fed, NUMA-aware placement, standardized PCIe Gen5 lane provisioning, separate GPU lines for training versus inference/fine-tuning, three-tier storage (NVMe cache, parallel file system, object storage), and a four-plane physical network design.

**Integrated operating model and validation** — The core claimed value is that liquid-cooled data center, HPC cluster, GPUaaS platform, and AI Agent as a Service are delivered in one space under one operating model, supporting both multi-tenant shared and enterprise-private environments on the same GPUaaS architecture. Cited from Chapter 6: a 957-GPU-node deployment where GPUaaS reportedly achieves bare-metal-equivalent performance while maintaining inter-organizational security isolation and resource control, with private deployments reducing time and cost versus self-building.

**Forward-looking roadmap** — AI infrastructure is treated as an ongoing target: rising power density across GPU generations, evolving resource-management standards such as Kubernetes DRA, and heterogeneous accelerators like NPUs. Stated plans include liquid-cooling designed for forward compatibility through next-generation GPU platforms (post-B300), technical review of extending GPU Live's dynamic allocation to heterogeneous accelerators, guaranteed-quota-based quantitative SLAs, more advanced topology-aware placement, and refined co-placement policies for training and inference.

**Intended audience** — Technical decision-makers evaluating AI infrastructure adoption, and architects/engineers designing and operating large-scale AI systems.

**Appendix (headings only, no content)** — 8.1 GPU specifications by model, 8.2 glossary of terms, 8.3 references.
